content.title: About
content.content: Celery juice is obtained by pressing fresh celery stalks (Apium graveolens). It has a light green color, a mild aroma, and a slightly salty taste. The juice is often consumed fresh as a tonic drink or used in culinary and detox programs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Celery belongs to the Apiaceae family and is grown in temperate climates.
Celery juice is more than 90 % water, making it an excellent hydrating beverage.
Ancient cultures used celery as a medicinal plant to aid digestion.
Celery can reduce body odor thanks to its volatile compounds.
The juice is a common ingredient in green smoothies and detox cocktails.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Celery juice contains vitamin C, quercetin, and other polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: Its high water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in blood pressure regulation and heart function.

items.title: Provides sodium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for nerve and muscle function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Phytonutrients and fiber in the juice promote normal bowel movements.

items.title: Celery allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The juice can contain notable amounts of sodium, which should be considered by people with hypertension.

items.title: Possible drug interactions
items.content: Celery may enhance the effects of certain anticoagulants; consult a doctor if you take such medications.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink celery juice freshly prepared, chilled or diluted with water. It can be added to smoothies, cocktails, soups, and sauces. A typical serving is 100–250 ml per day.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in an airtight bottle in the refrigerator for up to 3–5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions.

chicken-ns-as-to-part-rotisserie-ns-as-t.title: Chicken, NS as to part, rotisserie

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. The “rotisserie” form refers to cooking a whole bird on a rotating spit, which helps retain juiciness and flavor. The skin may be eaten or removed according to personal preference.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken provides all essential amino acids required by humans.
Rotisserie cooking distributes heat evenly, resulting in tender meat.
Chicken skin is rich in collagen, beneficial for skin and joint health.
There are countless cultural recipes for rotisserie chicken, from Mediterranean to Asian styles.
Free‑range chickens often have superior taste and texture.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken meat supplies complete protein that supports muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low fat (skin‑less)
items.content: Removing the skin dramatically reduces calories and saturated fat content.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is a good source of niacin, vitamin B6, and B12, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The high protein level helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter, so it must be cooked to an internal temperature of 165 °F (75 °C).

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: High sodium in processed products
items.content: Marinated or smoked chicken products often contain added salt.

items.title: Skin fat
items.content: Eating the skin adds saturated fat and extra calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rotisserie chicken can be served whole, sliced into portions, added to salads, sandwiches, or rice dishes. The skin can be left for a crispy crust or removed to reduce fat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags for 2‑3 months. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature.

classic-mixed-vegetables-canned-cooked-w.title: Classic mixed vegetables, canned, cooked with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Classic mixed vegetables are a blend of carrots, peas, corn and beans cooked in vegetable oil. The vegetables are blanched before being sealed in glass jars, preserving flavor, color and nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend is formulated for a balanced taste and texture.
The product is ready to eat straight from the jar.
Cooking in oil increases caloric value but enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Dark glass jars protect the contents from light, slowing oxidation.
A small amount of salt and spices is often added for flavor.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The vegetables provide vitamin B6 and folate, supporting metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene and vitamin C help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: The vegetable oil used contains monounsaturated fats beneficial for the heart.

items.title: Provides essential minerals
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in the mix help regulate blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Added salt may be a concern for people with hypertension; portion control is advised.

items.title: Caloric density from oil
items.content: The oil raises the energy content, which may be undesirable in calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oil
items.content: Some individuals may react to the type of oil used (e.g., sunflower oil).

items.title: Potential BPA in packaging
items.content: If the jar lid is coated with epoxy, bisphenol A exposure is possible; choose BPA‑free labeled products.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The vegetables can be eaten straight from the jar, added to salads, soups, stews, or used as a sandwich filling. They can also be gently warmed in a pan or microwave if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese, meat, tomatoes, and dark‑green vegetables, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of eggs prepared as an omelet or scrambled, combined with cheese, meat, tomatoes, and dark‑green vegetables (such as spinach or broccoli). An additional source of fat (butter, cream, or oil) is included to increase the energy content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are a complete protein source, containing all essential amino acids.
Cheese adds calcium and richness, while also increasing fat and calorie levels.
Meat (ham, bacon, or chicken) boosts iron and vitamin B12 content.
Dark‑green vegetables are rich in B‑vitamins, vitamin K, and antioxidants.
Added fat improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat provide complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Cheese and green vegetables supply calcium and vitamin K, which help maintain strong bones.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Tomatoes and green vegetables contain lycopene, lutein, and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy density
items.content: The added fat raises the calorie content, useful for individuals with higher energy needs.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A and D found in eggs and fat contribute to normal immune system function.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to eggs, cheese, or dairy fat.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Large amounts of butter or fatty meat can raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese and processed meat often contain salt; individuals with hypertension should monitor portions.

items.title: Caloric load
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑dense (approximately 500‑600 kcal per serving), so it should be balanced within the overall diet.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Beat eggs with a splash of milk or cream, stir in grated cheese, diced meat, tomatoes, and green vegetables. Heat oil or butter in a skillet, pour the egg mixture, and cook to the desired consistency, stirring occasionally.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a skillet or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned mackerel is fish caught in open seas, cleaned, cut into fillets and sealed in a metal can with added salt, vegetable oil, or tomato sauce. Mackerel is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, vitamins D and B12, and minerals such as selenium and iodine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mackerel belongs to the herring family and inhabits temperate and subtropical oceans.
Canning preserves the fish’s nutritional value for up to 3‑5 years without refrigeration.
In Japan, mackerel is often served as “saba” – grilled, but in cans it retains a soft texture.
Canned mackerel is one of the most affordable sources of omega‑3.
In Russia, canned mackerel is traditionally used in salads, sandwiches, and as a standalone snack.

items.title: Rich source of omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support heart health, lower triglyceride levels, and have anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: High vitamin D content
items.content: Vitamin D aids calcium absorption, supporting bone health and the immune system.

items.title: Vitamin B12 and selenium
items.content: B12 is essential for red blood cell formation, while selenium protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: Canned mackerel provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, making it a good choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Supports thyroid function
items.content: Iodine present in the fish is necessary for thyroid hormone synthesis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned products often contain high amounts of salt, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish or seafood.

items.title: Bisphenol A in packaging
items.content: Metal cans may have trace amounts of BPA; choose products from reputable manufacturers.

items.title: Potential contaminants
items.content: Like other marine fish, mackerel can accumulate mercury and other heavy metals; moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mackerel can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, pasta, rice dishes, or spread on bread. It can be gently warmed, but prolonged heating may reduce omega‑3 levels.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer the fish to an airtight container and consume within 2‑3 days, keeping it refrigerated.

content.title: About
content.content: Kimchi is a traditional Korean dish of fermented vegetables, most commonly napa cabbage, radish, carrot and a blend of spices. It has a spicy, slightly sour flavor and aromas of garlic, ginger and fish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kimchi is considered Korea’s national dish and is eaten daily by more than 90 % of the population.
Traditional fermentation can last from a few days to several months, depending on temperature.
There are over 200 varieties of kimchi, differing in vegetables and spice mixes.
Kimchi is often served as a side dish but is also used in soups, stir‑fries and pancakes.
In 2013 UNESCO inscribed kimchi on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Fermentation makes kimchi rich in live lactobacilli, which support gut health.

items.title: Vitamins B and C
items.content: The vegetables and spices provide vitamin C and B‑vitamins (B1, B2, B6) important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Garlic, ginger and red pepper contain antioxidant compounds.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Probiotics and vitamins together may enhance the immune response.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Kimchi is low in calories while delivering strong flavor.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Kimchi is often prepared with a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes include fish sauce; those with allergies should choose vegetarian versions.

items.title: Fermentation gas
items.content: Some people may experience bloating from excessive fermented foods.

items.title: Quality control
items.content: Improper storage can lead to growth of unwanted bacteria; always respect shelf‑life dates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kimchi is served as a side dish, added to soups (e.g., kimchi‑jjigae), rice dishes, pancakes and salads. It can be eaten fresh after fermentation or aged for a stronger flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store kimchi in an airtight glass jar in the refrigerator. When kept properly it remains good for weeks to months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or mold.

macaroni-or-pasta-salad-with-shrimp.title: Macaroni or Pasta Salad with Shrimp

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni or pasta salad with shrimp is a cold dish that combines cooked pasta, boiled or sautéed shrimp, fresh vegetables, and a light dressing made from mayonnaise, yogurt or olive oil. The salad offers a delicate seafood flavor, aromatic herbs, and a pleasant texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Short‑shaped pasta such as shells, penne or fusilli is usually used to hold the dressing better.
Shrimp are high‑protein and low‑calorie, making the salad diet‑friendly.
The classic recipe appeared in the United States in the 1970s as a light summer side.
Adding fresh herbs (parsley, dill, basil) boosts aroma and nutritional value.
The salad can be prepared ahead of time and retains its taste for up to 24 hours in the fridge.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: The dish combines modest fat and calorie levels, suitable for weight management.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Shrimp contain small amounts of omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Shrimp are a good source of vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta (if used) provides dietary fiber that promotes regular bowel function.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp are a common allergen; individuals with shellfish allergy should avoid this dish.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contain cholesterol; people with hypercholesterolemia should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium in dressing
items.content: Prepared mayonnaise‑based or soy dressings can be high in sodium; control added salt.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Shrimp must be fully cooked; raw seafood may harbor pathogens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a standalone dish or as a side to fish and meat. It is easy to eat with a fork or spoon and can also be used as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2 days. Stir before serving to redistribute the dressing.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp Garden Salad is a light dish made of shrimp, fresh lettuce, boiled eggs and a variety of vegetables (excluding tomato and carrot). It is served without dressing, allowing the natural flavors of the ingredients to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp are high‑protein and low‑calorie, making them a great choice for diet‑friendly meals.
The lettuce mix often includes romaine, arugula and spinach, which are rich in vitamins A, C and K.
Eggs add not only taste but also valuable nutrients such as choline and vitamin D.
Skipping dressing lets you control the amount of salt and fat in the dish.
The salad can be easily customized, for example by adding avocado or nuts.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Shrimp and eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A dressing‑free salad is low in calories, helping with weight management.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Leafy greens supply vitamins A, C, K and folate, while shrimp contribute zinc and selenium.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Shrimp contain modest amounts of omega‑3s, beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin D from eggs and zinc from shrimp help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp are a common allergen; individuals with shellfish allergy should avoid this dish.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs and shrimp contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw or undercooked shrimp can cause foodborne illness; always use fresh, properly cooked seafood.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: If shrimp are pre‑marinated, they may contain added salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, immediately after preparation. It can be enjoyed as a standalone meal or as a side dish. For extra flavor, a light squeeze of lemon or a drizzle of olive oil may be added.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Store shrimp and eggs separately from the leafy greens to maintain crunchiness.

content.title: About
content.content: Manhattan clam chowder is a thick, creamy soup made with milk and cream, featuring clams, potatoes, onions, carrots, and celery. The recipe originated in early 20th‑century New York and became popular for its rich flavor and velvety texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Unlike New England chowder, Manhattan chowder is prepared on a dairy base rather than a tomato base.
The earliest documented recipe dates to 1911 and appeared in New York culinary magazines.
The soup was often served in upscale seafood restaurants in the 1920s, regarded as a high‑class dish.
Traditionally fresh clams are used, but mass‑produced versions frequently rely on canned clams.
A common variation adds smoked bacon to enhance the smoky aroma.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Clams provide easily digestible protein that supports tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from the seafood helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Small amounts of omega‑3s contribute to heart health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: The creamy base supplies vitamin D, important for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Clams can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Cream and butter make the soup calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Canned clams often contain added salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Food poisoning risk
items.content: Improperly stored clams can harbor bacteria that cause foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, typically with croutons, fresh herbs, or crisp bacon bits. A squeeze of lemon juice can brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared soup in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When frozen, it can be stored for up to 2 months after cooling and portioning.

content.title: About
content.content: A meat taco without cheese is a classic Mexican snack consisting of a soft or crispy tortilla filled with seasoned ground meat, fresh vegetables, and spices. The absence of cheese makes it lighter and suitable for those avoiding dairy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “taco” comes from Spanish, originally meaning “plug” or “wad”.
Traditional tacos use beef, but chicken, pork, and turkey are also common.
Mexico boasts over 200 regional variations of taco fillings.
Tacos without cheese are often served with lime, salsa, and guacamole for bright acidity and creaminess.
Tacos gained widespread popularity in the United States in the 1920s through Mexican eateries and food trucks.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat is rich in vitamin B12 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Without cheese, this taco is suitable for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Fresh toppings like tomatoes, onions, and lettuce add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salsa and pre‑made seasoning mixes can be salty; individuals with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Meat fat
items.content: Fatty cuts of beef increase the calorie load; opting for lean cuts is recommended.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some people may be allergic to chilies, cumin, or other spices used in the seasoning.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Meat must be cooked thoroughly to prevent salmonella and other food‑borne illnesses.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tacos hot, folding the tortilla in half and filling it with meat, vegetables, salsa, and a squeeze of lime. Optional toppings include guacamole or lactose‑free sour cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared tacos are best eaten immediately. If needed, store the meat filling in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Tortillas should be kept in a dry place, sealed to retain crispness.
